item.title: Discussion: Improving the Fairness and Resilience of CKB Community Fund DAO Governance |关于 CKB Community Fund DAO 治理机制的一些思考与改进建议
item.dc:creator: yixiu.ckbfans.bit
item.description:
近期几个提案的讨论，让我重新思考了 CKB Community Fund DAO 当前的治理机制。有两个值得我们认真讨论的问题：第一阶段的社区讨论与点赞机制，以及第二阶段的实际投票权重分配。

关于第一阶段的讨论和点赞

我认为，讨论阶段的点赞行为很难通过明确的元规则（meta-rules）来有效约束。

原因其实很简单：

  • 论坛的注册门槛很低。

  • 点赞的门槛和成本也很低。

  • 我们很难判断不同时段、来自不同 IP 地址的不同账号，背后究竟是不是同一个人或同一个利益相关方。

这意味着， 如果有人真的想影响第一阶段的结果，他完全有可能通过一些看起来并无明显异常的账号和点赞行为来做到这一点。 即使事后发现了一些可疑行为，也不一定有足够的证据证明这些账号之间存在关联，更不用说证明它们受到了谁的指使。

我不认为我们有能力彻底解决这个问题：我们很难建立一套既能有效识别恶意行为，又不会误伤正常社区参与者的规则。 与其不断增加一些难以验证和执行的规则，不如保持现有相对简单的机制。

但这并不意味着第一阶段的点赞和讨论没有价值。恰恰相反，我认为讨论阶段真正重要的不是有多少人点赞，而是有多少社区成员愿意站出来，认真讨论提案的价值、质疑其中的问题，以及了解提案人和他们过去做过的事情。

这些讨论能够让更多人关注提案，也能帮助大家在进入第二阶段时做出更充分的判断。

我不太担心第一阶段的点赞数量，我更希望看到有更多社区成员参与讨论。

关于第二阶段的投票权重

相比第一阶段，我更担心的是第二阶段的实际投票。

从近期几个提案的投票情况来看，实际参与投票的人数似乎并不多，而且大部分参与者的投票权重相对较低。在这种情况下，少数拥有数千万 CKB 投票权重的持有者，就足以对最终结果产生决定性影响。

我不知道这是否应该被称为某种形式的 DAO governance capture（DAO 治理俘获），但我认为这至少暴露了一个DAO治理过程中值得关注的问题：当实际参与投票的人数有限时，少数大额持有者是否拥有了过大的决策影响力？

我并不反对大额 CKB 持有者参与治理，也不认为应该因为一个人持有大量 CKB 就限制他的投票权。

但目前的投票权重仅取决于 NervosDAO 的锁仓金额，这意味着，一笔今天刚刚存入 NervosDAO 的资金，和一笔已经在 NervosDAO 中锁定了几年时间的资金，在单位 CKB 上拥有相同的投票权重。

我觉得这才是我们当下最值得重新思考的地方。

一个早在 2023 年就有人提出过的想法

其实，类似的问题在社区里早就讨论过。

2023 年 1 月，@Yeti 曾发起过关于 Binance 和其他交易所、托管机构投票权的讨论：

(General discussion) The voting rights of Binance and other exchanges/custodians CKB Community Fund DAO
Edited to add Chinese translation @JackyLHH I wasn’t sure how to label this topic, please feel free to change if needed. What I would like to bring up for a general discussion (not a proposal) may not be a problem at this current time, but I believe that it is something that needs to be addressed sooner rather than later. If it isn’t dealt with now, then there is a real possibility that a time will come that it is impossible to fix in a decentralised way using the governance system. While I’…

当时讨论的一个重要问题是：交易所可能将客户托管的 CKB 存入 NervosDAO，然后利用这些资金获得投票权。但这些 CKB 的实际所有者是交易所的客户，交易所却可能按照自己的利益参与治理。

在讨论中，@JackyLHH 提出了一个值得研究的方向：借鉴 Coin Days （币天）的概念，在计算投票权时，不仅考虑 NervosDAO 的存款金额，还考虑存款持续的时间。

@Kumamon 也认同增加时间维度可能是一个好的方向。

@Yeti 对这个想法表示了赞同，同时也提出了一个值得注意的问题：**我们需要让小额持有者仍然觉得自己的投票有意义，否则当他们发现自己的投票在数学上几乎不可能改变结果时，就可能逐渐失去参与治理的兴趣。

我认为，这些观点在今天仍然具有参考价值。

是否应该给 NervosDAO 投票权增加时间维度？

我想重新提出这个方向，并希望社区能够进一步讨论它是否适合应用于当前的 CKB Community Fund DAO。

目前，投票权重仅取决于 NervosDAO 的锁仓金额。

我认为可以考虑引入一个时间系数：

Voting Power = Deposited CKB × Time Coefficient

也就是说，每一笔 NervosDAO 存款除了记录金额，还应该考虑它已经在 NervosDAO 中持续锁定了多长时间。

例如：

  • 一笔刚刚存入 NervosDAO 的 CKB，其时间系数应该很低，因此实际投票权重会被折扣。

  • 一笔已经锁定数月的 CKB，可以获得更高的时间系数。

  • 一笔已经锁定数年的 CKB，可以逐渐获得完整的时间权重。

具体的时间系数可以采用线性增长、递减边际增长或其他经过计算的模型，并设置合理的上限。

通过这样的机制将带来几个好处：

  1. 增加临时资本影响治理的成本。 即使有人在提案投票前临时购买大量 CKB 并存入 NervosDAO，也无法立即获得完整的投票权重。

  2. 鼓励长期参与。 长期将 CKB 锁定在 NervosDAO 中的持有者，可以随着时间推移获得更高的投票权重。

  3. 减少单纯依赖资金规模的治理优势。 让资金规模和时间承诺共同决定投票权重，而不是仅仅比较谁拥有更多 CKB。

  4. 为小额长期持有者提供更多参与空间。 让长期参与者的投票能够获得更有意义的权重，而不至于完全被短期的大额资金淹没。

当然，这并不是一个可以解决所有治理问题的方案。

例如，如果有人提前很长时间准备资金，时间权重依然无法阻止其影响投票。另一方面，时间权重也不能直接解决交易所托管资产的实际受益所有权与投票权归属问题。

此外，我们还需要考虑如何避免老资金长期积累过大的治理优势，以及如何在不同时间曲线之间取得平衡。

这些都需要进一步研究和模拟，但不应成为我们一步一步完善 DAO 治理机制的障碍。

最后

我希望借此机会重新开启关于 CKB Community Fund DAO 治理机制的讨论：

  1. 我们是否应该将 NervosDAO 存款时间纳入投票权重的计算？
  2. 如果引入时间系数，应该采用怎样的计算模型？是否应该设置最大计权时间？
  3. 如何在长期持有者与新进入生态的参与者之间保持平衡？
  4. 除了时间权重，我们是否还需要考虑其他机制，以避免少数大额持有者在低投票参与率的情况下决定治理结果？

我并不认为当前的治理机制存在什么根本性错误。相反，我觉得通过实际提案和投票，不断暴露问题，再逐步改进，本身就是社区治理应该经历的过程。

我们不能等到这些问题变得难以解决时，才开始认真讨论它们。

A good governance system should not only make decisions possible, but also ensure that the community has a meaningful voice in making those decisions.

以上只是我的一些观察和想法，希望听听大家的意见。

item.title: Receive CKB on Fiber without a channel or inbound liquidity
item.dc:creator: ebubedev
item.description:
People kept getting stuck on the same thing (esp. some of my Twine beta tester). They could create an invoice, and then nobody could pay it. No inbound liquidity, no route, and no obvious way to fix either one without finding a peer and opening a channel first.

That is what Fiber PR #1766 i opened adds to Fiber. A receiver with no channel can still be paid in CKB. The receiver registers with a liquidity node. The invoice names that node. If there is no route, the liquidity node opens a private CKB channel sized for that payment and forwards it once the channel is ready.

The pull request is open. It is not merged, and it is not in an official fnn release yet. Review is welcome on the PR.

Studio LSP

Studio LSP is the liquidity node I created and deployed for this. LSP means liquidity service provider: a Fiber node whose job is to open channels so another node can receive, and to sit on the other side of a channel when that node wants to send.

It is a normal Fiber node with a public address, funded with CKB, and configured as a just-in-time liquidity service. Your node still runs on your machine. Your keys stay with you. Studio LSP is the peer the payment uses.

It is a Fiber service, not a Fiber Studio feature. Any Fiber node that speaks this protocol can use it: fnn, fiber-wasm, and fiber-js. The repo has the testnet pubkey, the address, and the config to register your own node.

Two cases:

  • Receive, and you have no channel. Your node registers with Studio LSP. The invoice points at it. The sender pays Studio LSP, Studio LSP opens a private CKB channel to you, funds it, and forwards the payment. You end up with a channel and the CKB.
  • Send. You open a private CKB channel to Studio LSP with your own funds. Studio LSP accepts and locks 1,000 CKB on its side. That balance is what you can receive later on the same channel.

Trying it today

Official Fiber does not include this yet, so a released fnn cannot register with Studio LSP. Fiber Studio 1.1.6 is the current way to try it, because that build bundles the JIT branch. Once the pull request is in a Fiber release, the same Studio LSP works from any node. The connection steps are in the repo.

On testnet, with Fiber Studio 1.1.6 (Settings → Updates, or getfiberstudio.com):

  1. Start the node on testnet. It connects to Studio LSP on its own.
  2. Create a CKB invoice. A channel does not need to exist first.
  3. Have someone pay it. If you have no inbound route, Studio LSP opens a private channel and the payment lands.
  4. Add on-chain CKB when you want to send. The channel to Studio LSP is opened for you.

Limits on the testnet node

CKB only. UDT and Lightning are unchanged. Mainnet is not served by this node yet.

Testnet
Who pays when a receive has to open a channel The sender, 10 CKB
Smallest payment that can open a channel 100 CKB
Largest amount above the channel reserve 9,900 CKB
Inbound left after that first payment About 900 CKB, so a later receive can use the same channel
When you open a channel to send Studio LSP locks 1,000 CKB on its side

A receive fails if your node is offline, or if Studio LSP is offline or out of CKB. A second payment waits if the first channel is still opening. It does not reuse funding that was sized for the earlier payment.

If you want to try a receive with no channel, use the 1.1.6 build on testnet. If you run Fiber yourself, read the flow in PR #1766 and the node setup in studio-lsp. Comments on a receive that should have worked and did not are the most useful.

Confirm it

Update to Fiber Studio 1.1.6, start on testnet, and create a CKB invoice for 100 CKB. Leave the description empty or put “JIT test”. You do not need a channel open first. Paste the invoice in a reply here.

100 CKB is the smallest amount this node will open a channel for. I will pay each invoice when I see it. Keep your node running until the payment shows up.

item.title: Spark 和 Community Fund DAO 资助的差异浅析
item.dc:creator: zz_tovarishch
item.description:
近期发现 DAO 和 Spark 资助经常被放在一起讨论，虽然它们都是被放在 DAO & Funding 分类下，但两者是两个完全不同的资助项目：运作方式、资助金额、预期目标等都完全不同。以下为二者差异的浅析，也向社区简单汇报 Spark 的运营近况。

Community Fund DAO

CKB Community Fund DAO 规则和流程

CKB Community Fund DAO 是由 Nervos 社区发起，社区和基金会共同捐款的社区基金，用于资助社区成员围绕 CKB 生态进行如代码开发、活动组织、内容制作、宣传推广等促进生态发展的工作。

从这段描述可见，Community Fund DAO 采用的是去中心化治理模式，资助的范围多样，目的是促进生态发展。DAO 的每一笔资助都来自一个具体提案：任何人都可以按规则发帖，讨论阶段一周内获得 30 个赞后进入 Metaforo 投票，按 Nervos DAO 存款加权决定是否通过。

我是 DAO 的协调员，只负责流程，无权决定资助的倾向，DAO 本身也不会主动出资赞助某个项目或赛事。所以社区如果认为特定类型项目更值得支持，最合适的方式就有人提出这类提案，大家投票支持。如果想把对特定类型的资助倾斜变成制度，比如设立专项额度，则属于元规则修改，可以通过发起元规则提案的方式推进。

Spark

星火计划 (Spark Program) 小额资助方案

星火计划"(Spark Program)，是一项小额项目资助机制
…
支持开发者验证创意、打造 Proof of Concept 原型或进行 demo 迭代
…

通过小额资助让更多踏实的小创意快速成长，为未来申请更大型的资助打下基础

Spark 的定位和DAO完全不同，它的目标是支持概念验证、演示和种子用户测试这类早期工作，单个项目通常在一千美元上下，采用的是委员会审核制，成员包括 @Hanssen 、 @yixiu.ckbfans.bit 和 我， @xingtianchunyan 是协调员。虽然我们肯定希望所有获资助项目都能有长远发展，但对资助对象并不要求其在结项时就能被社区大规模使用或者直接具备生态、市场价值。

从 2025 年 5 月启动以来，Spark 金库收到 Eco Fund 注资1,886,792 CKB + 10,000 USDI（2025年5月15日，按当日CKB价格该笔注资计20,000 USD），Foundation 注资 7,220,216 CKB （2026年4月1日，按当日CKB价格该笔注资计10,000 USD）。在一年半的运营中，Spark 始终坚持透明和严格的审核，使用了约 90%的注资，收到了近100份申请，立项了24个项目，其中以应用类项目的早期探索为主。

已结项的项目除了本身通过Spark的资助完成小规模的初期探索，也为社区沉淀了大量经验。下面是部分项目对于社区和生态可复用知识的汇总，供社区查阅

已结项项目 开发者分享了什么
Dular 团队复盘了移动支付试点。结项报告记录了30名试点用户、57笔成功的 Fiber 支付和23份反馈。开发者还写到，商户关心钱能否在顾客与供应商之间接着流转，以及收款方离线时会遇到什么问题。试点心得 · 结项报告
Nervos Brain 团队把面向 CKB 开发者的知识问答工具放进 Nervos Nation 的 Telegram 群内测。作者公开了交付和测试结果，并说明真实用户评分和固定场景测试各自如何统计。开发者交付报告 · 群测说明
CKB-UGMP 开发者总结了做 Spore/DOB 铸造工具的初衷，比较了 IPFS、直接上链等存储方式，也分享了开发过程中对沟通和社区参与的体会。项目总结与心得
fiber-checkout 开发者对照原计划和实际交付，写了为何采用服务端代理、如何处理发票状态，以及结项后怎样持续检测上游更新对支付库的影响。开发者复盘 · 结项后维护记录
Blackbox 团队总结了硬件 POS 原型的测试方法、社区测试者发现的问题，以及下一轮硬件和交互设计要改什么。原型测试总结
WarSpore · Saga 开发者撰写了全链游戏的制作随笔、玩法和代币设计，也复盘了种子用户测试，并说明用户反馈和链上数据各自能支持哪些判断。游戏制作随笔 · 试点复盘讨论
Quantum Purse 开发者在访谈和 AMA 中讲了做抗量子钱包的初衷、技术选择和开发过程。开发者专访 · AMA 回顾
ckb-probe 开发者公开了用 eBPF 诊断 CKB 节点的性能实验和 RocksDB 案例，也记录了 WSL2 兼容性问题。性能评估与案例 · WSL2 排障记录
CKB Builder Lab 开发者公开了测试报告，并回应了下一步如何收集证据，判断这个工具是否真的帮助新开发者学习。开发者报告 · 对结项评价的回应
CKB Wallet Behaviour Intelligence 开发者解释了为什么把研究范围从判断钱包背后的身份，收敛为找出可复现的链上行为模式，以及数据能支持怎样的解释。开发者研究总结
CKB-VM Sail Validation Sprint 开发者说明了验证工具覆盖哪些指令和场景，也面向非技术成员撰写了文章，解释社区可以怎样参与复核。交付与验证范围 · 非技术成员如何参与
Progress Tracking Platform 项目的公开结项帖附有开发团队报告，可查阅进度追踪平台的交付记录。结项帖与团队报告入口
SoMo – Pixel Territory 开发者公开介绍了像素画布怎样使用 Spore、怎样定价的机制分析。开发者技术与试用介绍

此外，我们还看到，截至 2026 年 9 月 30 日，有 4 个项目在完成Spark后提交了 Community Fund DAO 资助提案，无论DAO投票的结果如何，这条路径验证了项目在完成Spark后，进一步成熟以获取更大资助的可行性。

综上，如果开发者的项目有合适的部分工作想申请Spark，我们非常欢迎，但是否获批仍要看具体提案，尤其是范围是否控制在Spark定位以内。申请方式请见 Spark 主帖。

item.title: Show Me the Use Case: Fiber Network Product Hackathon announcement!
item.dc:creator: neon.bit
item.description:
Show Me the Use Case: Fiber Network Product Hackathon

Build products for the next stage of Fiber

Registration for Show Me the Use Case: Fiber Product Hackathon opens soon!

This is the follow-up to the Fiber Network Infrastructure Hackathon. Where that hackathon explored gaps in Fiber’s supporting infrastructure, this one focuses on building compelling products on Fiber Network that address real user needs.

As a peer-to-peer payment network, Fiber offers a fast, low-cost alternative payment rail to traditional systems. It could support products across many areas, including regional and cross-border payments, gaming, social media, commerce and metered services.

We’re asking developers to think like entrepreneurs: connect their technical expertise with real-world challenges and business opportunities. Strong projects will identify a specific audience, make a case for user demand and product-market fit, and show how they will reach, engage and onboard users. User experience and a credible path to market are central to this hackathon. In order to help guide developers in this respect, we’ve partnered with BlockDev to provide access to seasoned experts from MDI Venture and BRI Venture.

Key details

Registration opens: 27 November
Pre-hackathon preparation and advice sessions: 30 November–4 December
Hackathon: 4–18 December
Duration: 2 weeks
All dates and deadlines: UTC
Platform: CKBoost
Prize pool: $20,000
Participation: Individuals and teams may enter; teams are strongly encouraged
AI tooling: Successful submissions may claim up to $20 as an AI tooling allowance
Registration: **Now live on CKBoost! **

Introduction

Nervos CKB is a proof-of-work Layer 1 blockchain built for flexibility, decentralisation and long-term extensibility. Its Cell model supports smart contracts, custom assets, ownership and verification logic, while its RISC-V-based virtual machine gives developers flexibility in choosing the cryptography and protocols they use.

Fiber Network is a payment-channel network for fast, low-cost, off-chain payments on CKB. It supports multiple asset types, including RGB++ assets and stablecoins, and creates opportunities for wallets, merchants, micropayments and other payment-focused services.

This hackathon, organised by Nervos Community Catalyst, is about putting that payment capability to work in products people can understand and use. The strongest ideas will start with a specific problem and audience, show why Fiber is useful to the solution, and explain how that audience will be engaged.

Mission brief

Build a user-facing product on Fiber Network that solves a real problem for a clearly defined audience.

Possible areas to explore include:

  • Regional and cross-border payments
  • Merchant checkout and commerce experiences
  • Gaming and digital goods
  • Social or community payments
  • Metered services and pay-as-you-go access

These examples are inspiration, not formal categories. All submissions will be judged together.

Who should participate?

The hackathon is open to CKB community developers and developers who are new to CKB. Participants may enter individually or as a team.

Teams are strongly encouraged, since developing a product often calls for complementary skills. Team size alone will not affect judging. A team will be required for projects seeking post-hackathon support, and there will be a Best Team prize.

Why participate?

  • Build a user-facing product on Fiber Network
  • Explore real payment problems across different industries
  • Develop and test a product idea with support from experienced advisors
  • Compete for a share of the $20,000 prize pool
  • Give prizewinning projects a chance to discuss their next steps with advisors from VC after the hackathon

Ecosystem partners

This hackathon, organised by Nervos Community Catalyst, is supported by the Common Knowledge Base Association, including teams from CKB Devrel, CKB, and Fiber. Alongside technical support, senior developers will give presentations during registration week on key topics for developers to get up to speed.

Furthermore, we’re working with BlockDev as our hackathon business advisory partner.

During registration week, BlockDev will announce presentations covering the essentials of building a blockchain startup and what makes a startup investable. Advisors include Markus Liman, venture capitalist and CEO of BRI Venture, and Alvin Evander, Vice President of MDI Venture.

After the hackathon, prizewinning projects will be invited to a further advice session with the advisors to help them consider the next steps in their journey.

Getting started

Use these resources to familiarise yourself with CKB and Fiber Network, and to find tutorials and examples to build from:

  • CKB documentation
    • Introduction to Nervos CKB
    • How CKB Works, including links to the Quick Start and dApp tutorials
    • AI resources and training tools
  • Community-contributed learning
    • Learning CKB: 24 lessons across 5 phases
    • Learn CKB in 45 minutes
  • Fiber Network
    • Fiber documentation
      • Fiber Storybook - Explaining Fiber Through Pico’s Airport Journey
      • Toolchain overview
      • Interactive tutorials - highly recommended!
    • Fiber Showcase, with open-source demos and community applications
    • Fiber Hackathon documentation, with resources, onboarding and tutorials
    • Fiber Network product demos:
      • Charge as you go - EV charging on Fiber
      • Fiber chat - decentralized social demo

To complete quests on CKBoost, you will need CKB testnet tokens. You can claim them from the Nervos Pudge Faucet.

Fiber setup and demos

Fiber LSP infrastructure will be available for developers to use, but there will be no shared public LSP service for this hackathon. Teams should plan to run the Fiber service their project needs locally, or run it on a public server if they prefer.

A publicly hosted product interface plus a video demonstration is sufficient. The video should show the product in action, including Fiber-connected functionality that may not be available through the hosted interface.

More detailed technical setup instructions will be shared before the hackathon.

Deliverables

Each submission should include:

  • Project summary
  • Target audience, market research, product-market fit and user acquisition strategy
  • Team name and members
  • Hosted product interface
  • Video demonstration
  • Technical breakdown, including an explanation of how the project uses Fiber
  • Future roadmap and go-to-market strategy
  • AI allowance claim, if applicable

Functional demos are required; written proposals alone will not qualify. Code does not need to be open source, but must be made privately available to the judges for review. Submissions should explain what is fully working and identify any parts that are mocked or simulated.

AI usage

You may use AI tools to research, develop and document your project. Successful submissions may claim up to $20 as an AI tooling allowance.

Use AI as an aid, and test and review your project throughout development to ensure it works as intended. We’ll be sharing more AI related tips and guidance over the pre-hackathon registration week.

Judging criteria

Projects will be assessed on:

  • Functional completeness
  • User flow and experience
  • Relevance to Fiber Network and CKB
  • Technical soundness
  • User friendliness
  • Market viability
  • Documentation quality
  • Practical usefulness
  • Potential for further development

Hackathon preparation checklist

  1. Think about a real problem, the people who experience it, and how your product could reach, engage and onboard them.
  2. Explore Fiber Network and decide how it could help solve that problem.
  3. Review the technical resources above and begin planning your project.
  4. Register through CKBoost when registration opens. Early registration will help you join the support channels and ask questions in advance.
  5. Plan your time across the hackathon dates so you can build, test and document a functional demo.

Support

The Build on CKB Telegram group will be the main discussion channel for hackathon-related questions and support. Participants will also receive information about support channels by email after registering.

The Fiber DevRel team will be available to assist with technical questions.

Rules

  • Individuals and teams may enter.
  • Only new projects are eligible for prizes. Pre-existing or repurposed projects are not eligible.
  • Projects must be viable user-facing products. Infrastructure-focused projects are not eligible for this hackathon.
  • Code does not have to be open source, but must be made privately available to the judges.
  • Plagiarism will result in disqualification and loss of prize eligibility.
  • All submissions must be made through CKBoost.
  • There can be no deadline extensions. Submissions added after the deadline without prior permission may be ineligible for prizes.

Prizes and deadline

The total prize pool is $20,000:

  • 1st place: $6,500
  • 2nd place: $4,000
  • 3rd place: $3,000
  • 4th place: $2,000
  • 5th place: $1,000
  • Commendation prizes: $500 each for five projects
  • Best Team: $1,000

Submissions close on Friday 18 December 23:59 UTC.

After the hackathon

As mentioned earlier, prizewinning teams will have the opportunity to discuss and receive advice from our hackathon partners who have a background in venture capital. This, however, is simply an initial step, and projects will be encouraged to move towards market viability and seeking further support where necessary.

I’m excited to see what the community produces. Good luck to everyone!

item.title: What Else Could a Cell Become ? [1]
item.dc:creator: ArthurZhang
item.description:
Polytype, Metatype, and the unfinished possibilities of the Cell model

I. Revisiting the Cell model

During CKCON 2026 last month, I found myself returning to a question I had encountered repeatedly whilst developing CellScript: how much does the author of one protocol need to know about another before the two can work together?

@Hanssen has approached this through SSRI, @xxuejie and @janx through CoBuild, @OWK50GA through IDL. In CellScript, I introduced ProtocolBundle to coordinate the requirements of independently developed contracts. @doitian had been wrestling with various aspects of this problem long before many of us began building on CKB.

Shortly before the conference, @jm9k asked me whether a Myelin session could run an enhanced Cell Model v1.5, with transaction structures and rules beyond those currently supported by CKB L1.

I gave him a technical answer and went back to writing code, but the question stayed with me. Curiously enough, I always had an intuition whilst developing Myelin that, sooner or later, certain applications would warrant an alternative Cell-like UTXO model, supported alongside the original CKB model. And this question has planted a seed in my mind, and i began to think more seriously about what such a model might look like, and what new possibilities it could open up.

It seems to me that the community have spent seven years learning how to build protocols around the Cell model. Suppose, for a moment, that we had the luxury of toying with the model itself, with everything we have learnt in the intervening years. Which of our architectural decisions would we make again? Which might we reconsider?

I began looking through some of the older Nervos discussions and found several ideas worth dusting off.

In August 2019, before CKB mainnet went live, Doitian published his Cell Model Changes Preview in v0.19.0, exploring a transaction structure in which Scripts and data were stored in separate collections, with Cells referring to their contents through hashes.

Although this representation did not survive into the Cell model we use today, I find the structural separation between a Script and the Cell referencing it rather interesting.


Figure 1. The 2019 design separated Script descriptions from Cell Outputs.

Two years later, Xuejie’s Extensible UDT explored a different aspect of the model. An asset could carry additional validation logic through a vector of extension scripts, allowing monetary conservation and supplementary policies to coexist within a single Type implementation.

The two proposals concern different things. The former explores how Scripts are represented and referenced; the latter explores how several validation programmes can jointly govern an asset. Read together, they invite an interesting architectural question about the relationship between a Cell and the programmes governing its evolution.

In 2022, Doitian’s assert proposal separated the conditions of a partial transaction from its signing mechanism. His subsequent And-Then pattern, drawing upon Xuejie’s earlier Chained Lock work, allowed several validation programmes to share a script slot. The OTX prototype developed by Doitian and Ethan in 2023 encountered some of the subtler security problems arising when independently constructed transactions intersect with existing Script Groups.

The 2024 article on ownerless contracts is particularly relevant to what I have in mind. Consider a protocol that wishes to enforce conditions on the creation of an asset whose Type slot is already occupied. Where should its validation logic reside? How can it work with an asset protocol whose author had no knowledge of its existence?

During the iCKB discussions in 2025, Jan proposed a common Meta Type capable of dispatching constituent scripts. Phroi went further, questioning the number of script slots altogether, exploring independent data regions and considering the storage implications of such a model.

Phroi also raised a similar question with me in April 2026, shortly after I introduced CellScript publicly. My answer at the time involved nothing more than companion Cells, receipts and explicit dependencies. I still consider these useful abstractions, particularly where separate state and independent lifecycles are desirable. Yet this left me wondering how much of this machinery we would need if the underlying Cell could express a richer set of relationships.


Figure 2. Selected historical explorations of script representation, validation, attachment and protocol composition.

Looking back through these discussions, I began to recognise two dimensions of composability.

One concerns how independent protocols discover one another, communicate their requirements and collaborate in constructing a transaction. Much of our work on CKB has been devoted to making this easier.

The other concerns the object itself. Can an asset become subject to several independently developed protocols, with each retaining its own identity, validation context and authority over its particular concerns?

I had often approached the second problem through the mechanisms available to the first. Perhaps it would be interesting to approach it from the Cell model instead.

II. Beyond a single Type

One of the things I have always admired about the Cell model is the distinction between Lock and Type. There is a rather profound idea embedded within this modest architectural decision: ownership and legitimate transformation are separate concerns.

I may own an object whose existence is governed by rules beyond my authority. A fungible asset belongs to me, but possession of its private key does not entitle me to increase its monetary supply.

Now suppose that I hold an asset subject to a vesting agreement and subsequently pledge it as collateral.

There are three protocols involved. The asset protocol governs issuance and conservation; the vesting protocol determines when certain rights become exercisable; the lending protocol governs the conditions under which the collateral may be released.

All three describe legitimate concerns about the same asset, and ideally their authors should be able to develop them independently.

On CKB today, we have several ways of constructing such an arrangement. We could introduce companion Cells, use a specialised Lock, devise a wrapper or seek cooperation from the asset’s existing Type implementation.

The appropriate choice depends on the application. Nevertheless, the author of a new protocol must often accommodate architectural decisions made by the author of an earlier one.

I became curious about a simpler and more intuitice arrangement. Suppose the asset retains its original monetary rules and acquires additional validation relationships throughout its existence. Each relationship is represented explicitly in the ledger.

I am tentatively calling this proposed model Polytype.

Figure 3. Independent constraints attached to a common Cell. Companion Cells remain useful wherever separate state or independent concurrency is required.

A Polytype Cell retains one Lock and an atomic unit of state, together with a collection of independently identified Types. Each attached Type contributes its own conditions for the legitimacy of a transaction.

For three Types, A, B and C, the admissible transactions satisfy:

The admissible transaction space is the intersection of the attached validators’ conditions.

The composition rule is deliberately simple. Given a common transaction context, every attached validator must accept the proposed transition.

(Of course, the intersection may be empty. Three perfectly respectable protocols, each behaving exactly as intended, could collectively produce an asset that nobody can ever spend. We would have invented a very sophisticated brick.)

III. Polytype

A Cell and its relationships

Returning to Doitian’s 2019 proposal, we might find some practical advantages in separating Script descriptions from the Cells that reference them.

A transaction containing many Cells governed by the same protocol has little reason to encode its complete Script description repeatedly. A transaction-level Script Dictionary could provide a compact representation, whilst the persistent ledger retains independently verifiable Script identities.

Figure 4. A possible Polytype encoding inspired by the 2019 Script collection. Dictionary indices are local to a transaction; persistent Script identities remain independently verifiable.

The choice between hashes, indices and other forms of reference is largely a matter of representation. We could explore any of these without altering the fundamental validation semantics of Polytype.

What matters semantically is that the relationship between Cells and Types becomes many-to-many. Each Cell can participate in several protocols, and each protocol can govern arbitrarily many Cells.

This has a particularly interesting consequence for something CKB developers are already familiar with: Script Groups.

Overlapping Type Groups

One of the virtues of CKB’s Type Script Groups is that they allow a programme to reason about several related Cells at once.

An asset validator, for instance, can examine a collection of consumed token Cells and compare their combined balance with that of the newly created Cells. The rules of monetary conservation are expressed over the group as a whole.

Under Polytype, a Cell may belong to several Type Groups simultaneously.

Consider two token Cells governed by the same monetary validator, A. One carries an additional vesting constraint, B, whilst the other carries a lending constraint, C.

Both belong to the conservation group of A. Their respective obligations are examined independently by B and C.

Figure 5. One proposed transaction induces three overlapping Type Groups. Monetary conservation is evaluated across all three Cells; the additional validators evaluate their respective groups. Acceptance depends upon the actual rules of B and C.

This is perhaps the most interesting property of the proposed model. An asset could acquire an additional policy without thereby acquiring a different monetary identity or becoming separated from its original conservation domain.

Validator A sees the Cells relevant to its monetary rules. B sees those participating in the vesting arrangement. C sees those participating in the lending agreement.

The runtime derives these groups from the complete Script identities and authenticated contents of the consumed and newly created Cells.

Doitian’s OTX research becomes especially relevant here. A validator’s understanding of which Cells belong to its group is part of its security model. Group membership must be derived independently of the transaction builder’s intentions.

There is, naturally, a question of data representation. Independently developed validators require compatible ways of interpreting the state they govern. Phroi’s earlier exploration of separate data regions deserves further attention in this regard.

I would like to establish the grouping semantics first. There is plenty of room to experiment with how the underlying data ought to be organised.

The evolution of constraints

An interesting consequence of Polytype is that the relationships between a Cell and its governing protocols can themselves evolve.

An asset may acquire a collateral constraint when pledged against a loan and discharge it upon repayment. An immutable-content validator might forbid its own removal, whilst a governance validator might permit its replacement under certain conditions.


Figure 6. The attachment and removal of a constraint are themselves validated state transitions. The asset retains its original logical Type identity throughout.

Since validation groups are derived from both consumed and newly created Cells, removing a Type remains subject to that Type’s own rules. The existing distinction between spending authority and validation authority is preserved.

This opens up a possibility I find particularly compelling: an asset created today could participate in a protocol invented years later, without its original developer having anticipated that particular relationship.

I think of this as a form of open-world composability.

IV. Metatype: an experiment on CKB

How much of the proposed semantics could we already express on CKB?

@janx’s earlier suggestion of a common Meta Type provides a particularly promising starting point. CKB’s RISC-V execution environment gives us considerable freedom to experiment with the interpretation of a Cell without changing the consensus-level structure of the Cell itself.

I would like to develop it a bit further here as a common composition mechanism occupying the ordinary Type Script slot. A Metatype Cell commits to a collection of logical Types, with the wrapper responsible for enforcing their validation.

The difficulty lies in preserving the grouping semantics described earlier.

Suppose two CKB Cells use Metatype, one carrying logical Types A and B, the other carrying A and C. Depending on their physical Script representation, they may belong to different CKB Type Script Groups.

Yet A must be able to reason about both Cells together.

Figure 7. Metatype reconstructs logical Type Groups across differently composed physical CKB Cells. M₁ and M₂ denote distinct physical Script identities in this example.

Simply spawning the constituent validators would leave this problem unresolved. A validator invoked through spawn does not automatically acquire a new understanding of its Script identity or the boundaries of its logical group.

Metatype must reconstruct the relevant groups across the transaction, deriving their membership from authenticated manifests and verifying that each participating Cell is subject to the appropriate enforcement mechanism. Each validator must then be provided with an execution context consistent with its logical Type identity and group membership.

The research objective can be expressed rather simply:

(Here, E translates a supported logical transaction into its physical CKB representation.)

Within the supported domain, the two environments ought to agree on the validity of the same proposed transition. Establishing this equivalence also requires Metatype to reject malformed representations and attempts to conceal or discard existing validation obligations.

Polytype and Metatype as two implementations of a common logical validation model. Establishing semantic equivalence between the two would itself be a worthwhile research objective.

There is a pleasant research opportunity here for a DSL such as CellScript as well. Contracts compiled against a sufficiently precise logical validation interface could potentially target both environments.

I am particularly keen to explore Metatype independently on CKB. Even if the native Polytype experiment never leaves the laboratory, there may be useful things we can learn and put into production on L1.

Where our existing work comes together

We can see that Hanssen’s SSRI provides a means for scripts to expose information and executable behaviour. Wilfrid’s IDL provides a vocabulary for describing interfaces. CoBuild and OTX concern the construction and authorisation of transactions involving independent participants. ProtocolBundle coordinates requirements arising from independently compiled contracts.

Figure 8. Protocol discovery, interface description, transaction construction, authorisation and validation within a common composition model. The layers indicate complementary responsibilities rather than mandatory dependencies.

Polytype and Metatype give these capabilities a more explicit object upon which to operate.

A validator might describe the evidence required to discharge an obligation. A wallet could discover this information and obtain suitable construction logic. Several protocols could contribute requirements to a partially constructed transaction, which could then be examined against their combined conditions.

I also find Phroi’s suggestion of interpreting Cell data through SSRI-like methods particularly intriguing.

An iCKB receipt, for example, might expose its economic relationship with CKB through a commonly understood asset interface, despite having a physical representation quite different from that of an ordinary UDT.

Given sufficiently expressive interfaces, an application might learn something meaningful about an unfamiliar asset without having been written specifically for it.

We would still have a great deal of work to do in establishing shared semantic conventions. Fortunately, many of the people I mentioned at the beginning of this article are already working on precisely these questions.

V. An open world of Cells

This brings me back to @jm9k’s question about Myelin.

Myelin was originally conceived around close compatibility with CKB’s existing transaction and execution semantics. With Cell Model v1.5 still very much a todo!(), one possible direction is to explore native Polytype in a fast PoS execution layer, with Metatype providing a corresponding representation on L1. A Myelin session might offer another environment in which to investigate some of the same validation semantics, albeit with different assumptions about state progression and settlement.

Figure 9. Native Polytype execution and Metatype enforcement on CKB. State authentication, settlement and exclusive spending authority require their own cross-layer mechanisms.

I find the prospect of an object travelling between these environments rather intriguing. An asset might undergo thousands of transitions elsewhere before returning to CKB. Ideally, the validators governing its behaviour could retain their logical identities throughout this journey, even as their physical representation changes.

Phroi has previously expressed reservations about general-purpose L2 development within the Nervos ecosystem. I do share his concern about devoting years to infrastructure that ultimately does little to improve what developers can accomplish on L1.

This is one of the reasons I am keen to give Metatype independent utility. An experimental execution environment could serve as somewhere to investigate more ambitious architectural ideas; the useful ones could find their way back into CKB through mechanisms available to us today.

I suspect some of our existing abstractions will survive this exercise remarkably well. Others may become simpler. A few may turn out to have been elaborate solutions to problems peculiar to the original arrangement of script slots.

Finding out which is which should be rather good fun.

item.title: Spark Program | Sigsheet: a unified standard for signing CKB multisig transactions
item.dc:creator: ILE_LABS
item.description:
Applicant: ILE Labs

Funding requested: $2,000 USD

Duration: 7 weeks, starting at approval (the first payment)

Payout address: ckb1qyqpkgfq00mzpsqh4e4gxpkdh3nafsepvl0qpddkyy

Contact: contact@ilelabs.org, Discord: emmzy_code01

In our own words

Our first application, ckb-msig, converted signatures between the formats CKB wallets already write. The committee’s answer was clear: instead of adapting to the fragmentation, design the standard that every tool can adopt. So that’s what we did. Sigsheet is one file and one set of rules for a CKB multisig transaction, and the specification draft, its test vectors and an independent check are already public. This grant turns the draft into a standard wallets can adopt: two libraries that implement it, in TypeScript and Rust, one tool that lets today’s ckb-cli and Neuron users sign while their wallets catch up, and a demo on testnet across all three tools.

1. Project Overview

What it is. Sigsheet is an open standard for signing a CKB multisig transaction: one canonical JSON file per transaction, and the rules every tool follows to read, check, sign, merge and finalize it. It’s what the committee asked for in its reply to our first application (t/11151 #2): “a unified standard for multisig signature formats — one that ckb-cli, Neuron, CCC, and other tools would collectively adopt.”

How wallets adopt it. Two libraries implement the whole standard and pass the same test vectors: TypeScript, for CCC apps and Neuron, and Rust, for ckb-cli and other Rust tools. A wallet adds one of them and signs with its own signer and keys. Its users can then co-sign with users of every other wallet that reads the file. Until a wallet does, one Sigsheet tool lets its users sign with the wallet as it is (section 4.4).

What it does for signers. Each signer uses the wallet they already have. Signatures are kept per lock group and per signer, so anyone can merge copies, in any order, with the same result, and nobody has to collect them. When enough members have signed, anyone finalizes the file into a standard CKB transaction.

Who it’s for:

  • groups whose members sign the same multisig with different tools: ckb-cli, Neuron or an app built on CCC;
  • payout signers, team treasuries and contract upgrades (section 3.2);
  • wallet and app developers, who get one tested format to support instead of one per tool, and a library that does the work (section 4.2).

At a glance:

  • Name: Sigsheet
  • Type: an open standard with open-source implementations (MIT)
  • Repository: ILE-Labs/Sigsheet, with the specification draft and the research behind it
  • Discussion: t/11298 on Nervos Talk
  • Duration: 7 weeks, one milestone a week
  • Phase: v0.1. v0.2 and v1.0 are open milestones (section 11).

2. Team Profile

ILE Labs builds open-source tools for CKB. For Sigsheet we:

  • wrote the specification draft and its 44 test vectors;
  • built the generator that rebuilds every vector byte for byte, and an independent check against CCC’s, ckb-cli’s and ckb-sdk’s own code and the deployed lock binaries;
  • tested today’s signing flows in ckb-cli, Neuron and CCC, and recorded every result on the research branch.

Everything, including this application’s milestones and issues, is public in ILE-Labs/Sigsheet.

3. Background

3.1 The problem

A CKB multisig transaction is signed by several people, often with different tools. Every tool and project that handles a partly signed multisig transaction keeps it in its own way. Our research (sections 4 to 6, and 11) has the details:

Tool or project How it keeps a partly signed multisig transaction
ckb-cli Its tx file, with the signatures keyed by lock args and no input cells, so it needs a node. Contract deployments use a separate deploy file
Neuron Its offline-signing file: the signatures are appended in the witness, and who has signed is in a map keyed by lock hash
CCC, and every app built on it No file: the signatures live in the transaction’s witness, in slots of a fixed length
ckb-sdk (Rust) No file: its signer puts each signature in the first empty slot of the witness
UTXO Global’s multisig wallet Its own server. Signing goes through one wallet, its own (website), and only the 2024 deployment is supported (server constants)
.bit’s signing site ckb-cli files only: “Invalid transaction data, only ckb-cli format is supported.” (ckb-multisig-wizard)
kuai “Currently kuai deployment contract only supports local signature deployment, which is a very bad experience when using multiple devices for multi-signature.” (kuai#276)
ChainPay Its own coordinator: “ChainPay coordinates partial signatures.” (chain-pay)
A 2024 proof of concept It converted ckb-cli and Neuron files, for the genesis deployment only. Its last commit was 2024-03-05 (ckb-multisig-cobuild-poc)
Two earlier shared formats An offline-signing draft (t/5794, 2021) and CKB Open Transaction (rfcs#406, closed unmerged). Neither became a standard

So signatures don’t move between tools. Both of these were measured in X1:

  • ckb-cli to Neuron. The incompatibility was reported in 2024 (neuron#3048), and Neuron added an import (#3169). But with Neuron v0.204.1’s own code, importing a ckb-cli file that held two signatures gave signatures: {}.
  • Neuron to CCC. CCC reads Neuron’s exported transaction, but turns its witness into 0x, which loses the partial signature.

So in practice:

  • one person collects the signatures from chat, PR comments or files, checks them by eye and assembles the transaction;
  • signers can’t check what they sign offline, from one file;
  • no tool covers all three multisig deployments. ckb-cli and Neuron don’t sign the 2024 deployment (design record, section 8.2, test 5). Its lock held 4,935,609.54 CKB in 93 live cells at block 21,098,567 (measured on 2026-11-24 with get_cells_capacity on a public mainnet node).

The problem isn’t making signatures. It’s making them portable, checkable and mergeable between tools.

3.2 Evidence of demand

The full list, with every quote, is on the evidence branch of our first project. These are the main ones.

Payouts take days or weeks.

  • A DAO payout (2-of-3) was started on Aug 21 and completed on Sept 4. In zz_tovarishch’s words, t/10583/20: “一位委员会成员在 8月21 该项目通过投票后，以2500/$0.00087= 2,873,564 CKB 发起了打款，随后在 9.4 其他委员会成员才完成了多签”. Translated: a committee member started the payment on Aug 21, after the vote, and only on Sept 4 did the other members complete the multisig.
  • The DAO said the same in 2024. JackyLHH, t/7849/1: “This is because DAO’s funds are stored in a multisig wallet, so it takes some time to collect signatures due to timezone and other factors.”
  • Spark pays every grant from a multisig (t/8752).

Contract upgrades run through PR comments. For Fiber’s v0.7.0 mainnet upgrade (fiber-scripts#34, 3-of-5), each signer ran ckb-cli deploy sign-txs and pasted the output into a comment, for one person to check and merge. v0.1 works on the transactions ckb-cli, CCC apps and Neuron build, not yet on ckb-cli’s deploy files.

Core developers asked for it.

  • doitian, ckb-cli#603: “Help users to prepare files for requesting multisig signatures from signers. Generate the tx json file and a markdown guidance for signers.”
  • doitian, ckb-cli#569: “It’s frustrated that sign-txs does not tell how to use the generated signatures”

Teams keep building their own: .bit’s signing site, kuai and ChainPay, in the table in section 3.1.

Neuron users get stuck.

  • jordanmack, neuron#2907: “I tried to send and I can’t figure out how to sign and broadcast.”
  • rink1969, neuron#3260: offline multisig on a transaction that mixed locks ended with “报签名失败” (translated: signing failed).

Bitcoin solved this with one shared format. PSBT (BIP-174) “holds the signatures for an input while the input does not have a complete set of signatures”, and wallets interoperate through it. CKB has no such standard. Sigsheet is that standard for CKB.

3.3 What changed since our first application

The committee gave two reasons (t/11151 #2), and this is how Sigsheet answers each:

  1. “signers must still collect all signatures and forward them to a single individual for aggregation”. In Sigsheet there’s no collector role. The file passes from signer to signer, or each signer posts a copy and anyone merges the copies, with the same result in any order. In v0.1 each signer still receives the file and passes it on, so the coordinating is reduced, not removed (design record, section 10). v0.2’s optional relay carries one signature at a time, so wallets can deliver them automatically.
  2. “design and propose a unified standard for multisig signature formats”. That’s Sigsheet: a public specification with test vectors, not a converter. ckb-msig adapted to each tool’s format. Sigsheet gives every tool one format to read and write, and two libraries to adopt it with.

4. Solution

4.1 The standard

A Sigsheet file carries everything a signer needs to check what they sign, offline and from the file alone (spec, section 1):

  • the unsigned transaction, and the witness templates of its lock groups;
  • every previous transaction its inputs spend, so each input cell is checked by hash;
  • the headers and inclusion proofs a Nervos DAO withdrawal needs;
  • the multisig configs;
  • every signature so far, keyed by lock group and signer.

The rules every implementation follows:

  • one canonical form (RFC 8785), so the same file has the same bytes everywhere;
  • 31 reader checks, so every tool refuses the same bad files;
  • a lock’s kind comes from the chain, never from the file: the code hash and hash type of the cell it spends (spec, section 6.1);
  • each lock’s own signing message, computed from the file alone;
  • a merge that gives the same bytes in any order, and a finalize that writes the standard transaction;
  • the three multisig deployments (genesis, 2024 and v2) and the single-key lock. New lock kinds are added without a format change (spec, section 12).

The final transaction uses the existing CKB locks. Sigsheet needs no new on-chain script and no change to existing multisig addresses.

4.2 How a wallet adopts it, and why it would

How. A wallet adds Sigsheet with one of the two libraries. The languages match the main CKB tools: TypeScript, on @ckb-ccc/core, for CCC apps and Neuron; Rust for ckb-cli and other Rust tools. Then:

  1. Open a Sigsheet. The library reads the file and runs every check.
  2. Show the signer what they’re signing, derived from the checked data: the outputs, the inputs and their cells, and each group with its members.
  3. Sign with the wallet’s own signer. The library gives the wallet each group’s signing message. The wallet signs it the way it signs today, with its own keys, and the library adds the signature. Keys never leave the wallet.
  4. Share it. Merge copies, and finalize once enough members have signed.
  5. Prove it. Run the 44 test vectors. Passing them means the wallet gives the same bytes as every other implementation.

At design stage, adding Sigsheet inside each wallet was a small change. It took 381 code lines in ckb-cli (plus 87 for creating a file), 229 in CCC and 137 in Neuron, and each wallet’s own tests gave the same results before and after (X6).

It works with CCC as it is. The TypeScript library is its own package on @ckb-ccc/core as published, so any CCC app can add it today, with nothing to merge into CCC and nothing to wait for. That’s where it sits after our discussion with CCC’s maintainer on ccc#646.

Why a wallet would adopt it:

  • Its users can sign with everyone else’s. One format means a wallet’s users co-sign with the users of every other wallet that reads it, with no converter for each pair of wallets.
  • The hard parts come done. The canonical form, the 31 reader checks, the 18 attack cases, Nervos DAO withdrawals and the three multisig deployments are all specified and covered by the test vectors. A wallet doesn’t design or maintain any of it.
  • Its signers can check what they sign, offline. The file carries every previous transaction, so the wallet can show each input cell without trusting a node.
  • It keeps its own signing. The wallet signs with its own code and keys. The standard only fixes what the message is.
  • It’s small and open. The change was small at design stage (above), the specification and the libraries are MIT, and nothing is hosted.
  • The interim tool steps aside. Once a wallet reads Sigsheet itself, its users don’t need the Sigsheet tool.

4.3 How it’s used

  1. A signer’s tool creates a Sigsheet for a multisig transaction.
  2. Each signer’s tool reads the file and runs the checks.
  3. The signer reviews what the transaction does, and signs their group with their own wallet.
  4. The signed file is passed on, or posted as a copy.
  5. Anyone merges the copies. Any order gives the same file.
  6. When enough members have signed, anyone finalizes it into the transaction to send.

4.4 Until wallets adopt it: the Sigsheet tool

Nothing in v0.1 waits for any wallet’s maintainers. Apps built on CCC sign with the TypeScript library directly. For the wallets that don’t read Sigsheet yet, one Sigsheet tool opens the file, checks it, and shows what’s being signed. Then it gets the signature from the signer’s own wallet, through that wallet’s own file: the official Neuron through its offline-signing file (neuron#3518), and the official ckb-cli through its tx file (ckb-cli#694). Neither wallet is changed, and no key passes through the tool.

  • What it adds: one step for those signers (sign in the wallet, then bring the signature back), which native support removes. ckb-cli’s signing reads the input cells from its node, as it does today.
  • Where today’s wallets fall short. The standard and both libraries handle these cases. The tool can only pass on what a wallet signs:
    • Neuron v0.204.1 leaves the witnesses beyond the inputs out of its signing message, so its signature on such a transaction doesn’t verify (X1). The tool holds those files back from Neuron signers, who sign them in ckb-cli or a CCC app instead, and we offer Neuron the fix as a pull request.
    • The official ckb-cli and Neuron don’t sign the 2024 deployment at all. Sigsheet’s libraries handle it, so a 2024 multisig is signed in a wallet or app that uses one, such as a CCC app with the TypeScript library.

It isn’t a bridge. Wallets don’t talk to each other through it. Every wallet writes to the same file, and anyone merges the copies. When a wallet adopts the standard, its signers don’t need the tool. The README’s questions explain why one file and one tool work where a bridge doesn’t.

4.5 Why a new format, not an existing one

We tested the alternatives before writing the spec (paths):

  • Converting between today’s formats is what ckb-msig did, and the committee asked for a standard instead.
  • Keeping partial signatures inside the transaction’s witness, as CCC does, depends on the order of the files.
    • Our test case was Fiber’s v0.7.0 upgrade, a 3-of-5 multisig with five signatures. Merging the five copies with CCC’s aggregateTransactions in all 120 orders always gave a valid multisig witness, but 60 different ones: it kept the first three signatures in file order.
    • The single-key input’s signature survived only in the 24 orders where its copy came first (X3a, section 1).
  • Sigsheet keeps each signature by lock group and signer until the end. That rule gave the same result in 2,000 of 2,000 design-stage trials (X3a, section 2).

5. What’s already built

The MVP is complete (milestone):

  • the specification’s first draft;
  • 44 test vectors: 24 cases, 18 attacks and 2 mainnet transactions. Each case holds the file as created, one copy per signature, the merged file, the final transaction and its expected results. Each attack says whether a reader must refuse it or drop its signatures;
  • the generator, which rebuilds every vector byte for byte;
  • an independent check: CCC’s, ckb-cli’s and ckb-sdk’s own code, and every final transaction run through the deployed lock binaries under ckb-debugger, with negative controls that must fail as the chain does;
  • the checks on Linux, macOS and Windows, on every pull request.

The research is on the research branch: the design record, the experiments, and the design-stage wallet patches and benchmarks.

The feedback so far:

  • The spec is open for comment in t/11298, and has been shared with ckb-cli’s and Neuron’s maintainers (ckb-cli#694, neuron#3518).
  • On ccc#646, CCC’s side found three problems, and we’ve accepted all three for v0.1:
    • the Nervos DAO deposit-header index is read two ways, by the DAO script and by the node’s fee calculation;
    • a merge can produce a file a reader refuses, by going past the 255-signature limit for a carried group;
    • the CoBuild profile’s round trip covers fewer files than the draft said.

6. What this grant pays for: seven weeks

Each week is a GitHub milestone, and each task is an issue with its own acceptance test.

Week Milestone Tasks
1 TypeScript reference implementation on CCC: read, check and show #9 read, check and show a file
2 TypeScript reference implementation on CCC: sign, merge, finalize, create and send #10 sign, merge and finalize; #11 create and send
3 Rust library: read, check and show #12 read, check and show a file
4 Rust library: sign, merge, finalize, create and send #13 sign, merge and finalize; #14 create and send
5 The Sigsheet tool, with the official ckb-cli and Neuron #16 sign in the official Neuron; #17 create a Sigsheet from Neuron’s export; #15 hold back files Neuron can’t sign, and offer Neuron the fix; #55 sign in the official ckb-cli, and create a Sigsheet from its tx file
6 Testnet demo with all three tools #18 each tool reads and signs the files the other two create; #19 the testnet demo, with every transaction hash published
7 Spec v0.1, the documentation, the benchmarks re-run and v0.1.0 #20 answer every comment and list the changes; #21 specification v0.1; #25 all ten acceptance tests in one command, and the benchmarks re-run; #52 the documentation; #26 the v0.1.0 tag

The testnet demo puts a 2-of-3 genesis multisig and a 3-of-5 v2 multisig on testnet, signed across the tools: once passed from signer to signer, and once posted as copies and merged by someone who isn’t a signer.

7. Required Funding and Breakdown

$2,000 in total, by week and task:

Week Task Cost
1 #9 read, check and show $170
2 #10 sign, merge and finalize $170
2 #11 create and send $110
3 #12 read, check and show $130
4 #13 sign, merge and finalize $150
4 #14 create and send $120
5 #16 sign in the official Neuron $110
5 #17 create from Neuron’s export $50
5 #15 hold back files Neuron can’t sign, and the fix for Neuron $60
5 #55 sign in the official ckb-cli, and create from its tx file $80
6 #18 the cross-tool record $200
6 #19 the testnet demo $150
7 #20 answer the feedback $50
7 #21 specification v0.1 $100
7 #25 the ten acceptance tests and the benchmarks $100
7 #52 the documentation $100
After v0.1.0 Six months of maintenance: a reply within 72 hours to issues and feedback, fixes to v0.1, dependency updates and documentation $150
Total $2,000

Why the weeks differ:

  • Week 1 ($170) is the reader of every rule: the canonical check, the 31 checks, the lock kinds taken from the chain, and what a signer is shown.
  • Week 2 ($280) completes the reference implementation: signing through CCC’s signers, the merge, ready and finalize, and creating and sending with a node. The Sigsheet tool is built on it.
  • Week 3 ($130) is the same reader in Rust, giving the same results as the TypeScript library on every vector.
  • Week 4 ($270) is signing through a signer the wallet provides, the merge and finalize in Rust, and creating and sending.
  • Week 5 ($300) is the Sigsheet tool, built on the TypeScript library. The work is the two wallets’ own files, reading their signatures back, and the fix offered to Neuron, with Neuron’s own tests.
  • Week 6 ($350) runs every pairing of the three tools on a devnet, then the testnet transactions.
  • Week 7 ($350) is the specification after the feedback, the ten acceptance tests in one command, and the documentation.

Why above $1,000. One standard that three tools, in two languages, must implement and check against shared test vectors, on the genesis, 2024 and v2 deployments. With $1,000 we’d build the two implementations (Weeks 1 to 4, $850) and stop there: no Sigsheet tool for ckb-cli and Neuron signers, no cross-tool testnet demo, and no specification v0.1 from the feedback.

Payment. 20% ($400) at approval. The rest in parts at the weekly check-ins, each a closed milestone with its results shown, or after completion.

8. Deliverables and How to Verify

Each week closes a milestone whose issues say how they’re verified. Most checks need no code reading:

  • Transactions: the testnet demo’s transactions are published with their hashes and the tool behind each signature, so any explorer shows them (test 8).
  • One command: a single command runs all ten acceptance tests (design record, section 8.2). The tests:
    • both implementations reproduce every vector byte for byte;
    • each attack is refused, or its signatures are dropped;
    • a merge in at least 200 random orders gives one result;
    • every check runs with networking off;
    • each tool reads and signs the files the other two create;
    • a genesis multisig with N ≥ 11 passes a node’s pool check;
    • each wallet’s own tests pass before and after its change;
    • the testnet transactions;
    • the feedback, with its list of changes;
    • the Nervos DAO case.
  • A record: for every pairing of tools, the files, their hashes and the committed devnet transactions are kept in the repository.

v0.1.0 is tagged only when all ten pass at that commit.

9. Maintenance

For six months after v0.1.0, ILE Labs maintains the release:

  • a reply within 72 hours to every new GitHub issue in the repository, and to every comment on this thread and on the spec thread (t/11298);
  • triage of reported issues;
  • fixes to v0.1;
  • corrections to checks or compatibility found in real use;
  • dependency updates;
  • the documentation and the test instructions.

This doesn’t promise new features. The repository stays open to contributions and review.

10. CKB Alignment

  • It builds on what CKB already has: the existing multisig and single-key locks on all three deployments, and the standard transaction, with no new on-chain script.
  • Adopting it is small, and stays in each wallet’s hands: a library, the wallet’s own signer, and the shared test vectors.
  • It’s meant to become a CKB standard. v1.0 is a stable specification with a conformance suite any implementation can run, proposed as a CKB RFC.
  • It helps the people who sign CKB’s shared funds: payout signers, team treasuries and contract upgraders, whatever tool each member uses.

11. After Spark: the roadmap

These are open milestones, published before this application:

  • v0.2:
    • a readable summary for signers;
    • a command that writes the file and that summary in one step, in the Sigsheet tool and offered to ckb-cli;
    • an optional relay that carries one signature at a time, about 367 bytes at design stage, instead of the whole file;
    • Omnilock’s multisig mode;
    • Neuron’s own Sigsheet screens, offered to Neuron as pull requests;
    • support in more tools.
  • v1.0: a stable specification with a conformance suite, proposed as a CKB RFC.

Questions we expect

Why would a wallet adopt Sigsheet, and how much work is it?

  • Why: its users can then co-sign with the users of every other wallet that reads the file. The checks, the attack cases, Nervos DAO withdrawals and the three deployments come specified and tested, and the wallet keeps its own signing and keys.
  • The work: one library, the wallet’s own signer, and the 44 test vectors to prove it. At design stage the change was 381 code lines in ckb-cli, 229 in CCC and 137 in Neuron (section 4.2).

Isn’t the Sigsheet tool a bridge, like ckb-msig?

  • No. ckb-msig converted between the formats wallets already write, and someone stayed in the middle.
  • With Sigsheet, wallets don’t talk to each other through the tool. Every wallet writes to the same file, and anyone merges the copies.
  • The tool is a signer’s way in, for wallets that don’t read Sigsheet yet. Two libraries, in TypeScript and Rust, let any wallet read it natively, and then its signers don’t need the tool.
  • It’s one week of seven: $300 of the $2,000. The rest pays for the two libraries, the cross-tool demo, specification v0.1 with its tests and documentation, and maintenance.

Does Sigsheet need CCC, ckb-cli or Neuron to change?

  • No. The TypeScript library is its own package on @ckb-ccc/core as published, so any CCC app can use it today. On ccc#646, CCC’s maintainer said CCC currently has no plans to include Sigsheet itself, and welcomed progress updates here on Nervos Talk.
  • ckb-cli’s and Neuron’s maintainers have the spec (#694, #3518), and nothing in v0.1 waits for them. If maintainers later agree to include Sigsheet, ILE Labs will say so in a comment on this thread.

What if ckb-cli and Neuron never include it? Then their users sign with the official ckb-cli and Neuron, through the Sigsheet tool. Every file is the same Sigsheet, checked against the same vectors.

Why not a hosted multisig wallet? A hosted wallet removes the exchange when every member uses it, and its server holds the transactions and signatures. Sigsheet is for groups whose members sign with different tools, on any of the three multisig deployments, with nothing hosted. v0.2’s optional relay automates delivery for those who want it.

Isn’t this the same as tools that check a transaction before signing? Checking the inputs is one part of Sigsheet. The file carries every previous transaction, and each is checked by hash. Sigsheet’s main job is the part one signer can’t do alone: signatures from different tools in one file, kept per signer, merged in any order with the same result, and finalized by anyone.

Is it safe to use for funds?

  • Sigsheet never signs and holds no keys. Each signer signs in their own wallet.
  • A reader takes each lock’s kind from the chain, never from the file.
  • A signature that doesn’t verify for this exact transaction isn’t accepted.
  • Each of the 18 attack vectors says what a reader must do: refuse the file, or drop its signatures.
  • The chain checks every signature again.

Who uses it first? Groups whose members already sign in different tools: payout signers, team treasuries and contract upgraders (section 3.2). v0.1 works on the transactions ckb-cli, CCC apps and Neuron build, not yet on ckb-cli’s deploy files.

item.title: Oracell: Contention-Free Witness Oracle for Nervos CKB (Phase 1 MVP Live on Pudge — Feedback Welcome)
item.dc:creator: RikoKurnia
item.description:
Hi everyone,

I’ve been working on Oracell, a contention-free oracle infrastructure built natively for Nervos CKB’s Cell Model as part of the CKB Builder Track (Week 11–12). Following initial architecture discussions, Phase 1 (MVP) is now live on Pudge Testnet (rikokurnia/oracell on GitHub, live app at oracell [dot] vercel [dot] app), and I’d love to gather technical feedback from the wider CKB community before moving into Phase 2.

The Problem We’re Solving

Traditional push-based oracles map poorly onto CKB’s Extended UTXO (Cell) architecture:

  1. Cell Contention: Updating a single shared price cell destroys its previous OutPoint, causing concurrent DeFi liquidations or swaps referencing that cell in the same block to fail.
  2. Cherry-Picking / Stale Quote Risks: Because CKB-VM scripts execute deterministically without access to global block height or wall-clock time, loose signature windows allow latency arbitrage against older quotes.
  3. Capacity Rent: Requiring every consuming dApp to maintain and mutate its own on-chain price cell increases state rent and cycle overhead.

Phase 1 Architecture & What’s Live

Instead of mutating a shared oracle cell, Oracell delivers signed multi-source market quotes (aggregated from CEX feeds with CKB anchor metadata) directly through the transaction witness:

  • Stateless Witness Verification: @oracell/sdk packs a 184-byte BIP-340 Schnorr proof into WitnessArgs.output_type without consuming any shared oracle cell—allowing parallel transactions in the same block with zero contention.
  • Tip-Header Binding (header_deps): Each quote commits to a recent CKB block hash. The on-chain RISC-V verifier (oracell-verifier) enforces a two-block freshness window relative to supplied header_deps, while the SDK proof runner checks the live RPC tip at submission.
  • Hosted API & SDK: Both ESM and CommonJS clients of @oracell/sdk work out of the box against our hosted /api/oracle/feeds and /api/oracle/quote endpoints without requiring a local server.

Verified Pudge Proof & Benchmarks

  • Code Cell Deployment (Pudge): Tx 0xb2834f4487155d69fa5780a40819196cca1f818a3e62175bb9f2f39a7aeac0b1 (Block 23,135,440, 102,616 bytes RISC-V ELF, data2)
  • Confirmed Consuming Transaction: Tx 0x14beb0d8c0bc0b2a2f1c4aa788c3171284b4c5443074a28059e234cc5bf0ee90 (Block 23,135,450, 5,530,230 RPC cycles)
  • CKB-VM Emulator Contention Benchmark:
    • Shared-cell baseline: 1 / 20 transactions admitted (19 cell contention conflicts)
    • Oracell stateless witness: 100 / 100 transactions verified (0 conflicts, 3,886,926 cycles per verification)
  • References (plain text while my new account’s link limit is still active):
    • GitHub Repository: rikokurnia/oracell (commit fb9f0b5, see contracts/DEPLOYMENT.md)
    • Live Explorer & Sandbox: oracell [dot] vercel [dot] app (/markets, /docs, /sandbox)
    • CKBuilder Technical Review Issue: Nervos-Community-Catalyst/CKBuilder-projects Issue #57

Explicit Phase 1 Boundaries

To be completely transparent about current limitations:

  1. Single Publisher Key: Phase 1 uses a single pinned BIP-340 Schnorr publisher key. Distributed key generation (DKG), threshold Schnorr aggregation (MuSig2 / FROST), and CKB collateral staking/slashing are scoped for Phase 3.
  2. Relative header_deps Freshness: Because CKB-VM cannot read global state or the live network tip, the on-chain two-block window is evaluated relative to the transaction’s supplied header_deps. In production DeFi/L2 flows, this is paired with client/co-signer tip verification at submission time.

Looking for Community Feedback (Next Phases)

Before scoping a follow-up milestone (Phase 2), I would appreciate feedback from CKB developers on three questions:

  1. CellScript Integration: Would a native CellScript helper/module for consuming Oracell’s 184-byte witness proof be useful for teams building CKB-Native DeFi protocols?
  2. Fiber Network & Perun Use Cases: For builders working on Fiber or Perun, is there active demand for discrete Schnorr nonces / DLC adaptor attestations for conditional swaps, hedging, or dispute resolution?
  3. Testnet Early Adopters: Are any teams building on Pudge interested in testing @oracell/sdk in a live dApp (lending, DEX, or hedging) and sharing integration friction points?

Thanks in advance for taking a look—any critique on the verifier design, witness format, or roadmap priorities is very welcome.

item.title: Crowns: a live 3D car race on CKB where the chain is the referee
item.dc:creator: Kaylah
item.description:
Hi everyone I’m Chioma, a builder in the CKBuilders program. I’ve been building Crowns, a real-time 3D car race where players put CKB on the line and the chain decides who won. It’s live on testnet, and I’d love for you to race it and tell me what you think.

Play: https://keepers-relay.vercel.app (testnet)
Code: GitHub - Kaylahray/keepers_relay: Crowns: live 3D car races on Nervos CKB. 2–5 players race 3 laps for a shared pot; each phone signs its own moves, and the chain replays the whole race before paying the winner. Rust rules on CKB-VM and in WebAssembly, Spore trophies, testnet. · GitHub
Build thread: Crowns: a live multiplayer skill game where CKB-VM replays every run · Issue #45 · Nervos-Community-Catalyst/CKBuilder-projects · GitHub

Why I built it

In most online games with money on them, you have to trust the server. It holds the money, it decides who won, and you can’t check either. I wanted a fast, real-time game where nobody has to be trusted: not me, not the server. The chain holds the money and replays the race itself before it pays anyone.

What it is

A race for 2 to 5 players: 3 laps, everyone driving at the same time, with items, boosts and crashes. Races come in two kinds:

  • Entry races: everyone puts in the same entry fee in CKB, and the winner takes the whole pot.
  • Sponsored races: the host puts up the prize and you join free. You only lock a deposit for your seat, and it all comes back after the race.

In the game:

  • 3 tracks: Harbour Loop (the fast one), Switchback Hill (tight hairpins) and Old Town (narrow streets), each with its own scenery.
  • 8 items from pads on the road: Ram, Slick, Jolt, Barricade, Crown Rush, Ward, Patch and Draft. Crashes and hits cost health, and a wrecked car stops for a moment before it rejoins.
  • Phone or computer: on a phone, touch the left or right side of the screen to steer, with buttons for boost and brake. On a computer, use the keyboard.
  • Free practice against two bots on the same rules, with no wallet.
  • Trophies: win a race and claim a trophy, a Spore you own. You can only get one for a race you really won, and the CKB inside it stays yours.
  • Profiles: claim an @username, which is a cell you own on chain. Upload a picture or pick a ready-made look, and it’s minted as a Spore you own and set as your profile picture. Your trophies, wins and crown shards show on your profile and on the leaderboard.
  • Replays: anyone can open a finished race, see each driver’s time, shards and moves, and watch it again in 3D, rebuilt from the moves stored on chain.

How a race works

  1. Host: someone opens a race and picks the track, the number of seats and when it starts (5 to 60 minutes). They either set an entry fee, or sponsor a prize and let players in free.
  2. Join: players take a seat. Each player who joins takes a fifth off the time left.
  3. Start: when the clock reaches zero, everyone is taken into the race at the same moment, with a 10-second countdown.
  4. Payout: when the race ends, the winner is paid automatically. If nobody finishes, everyone gets their money back, and a sponsor gets their prize back.

Your wallet only asks you once, when you join. While you race, your browser signs your moves with a temporary session key, so there are no popups mid-race.

How CKB makes it fair

  • No one holds the money. The host’s CKB sits in a match cell and each player’s in their own seat cell, all locked by the match script, live-match. Not me, not the server.
  • The chain is the referee. The finish transaction carries every car’s moves. live-match spawns the game script with ckb-script-ipc and calls it like a function: judge(record) replays the whole race tick by tick and returns each car’s place. Only then does live-match pay out.
  • Nobody can fake a win. Each player’s moves are signed by their own session key, and the script checks the winner’s signature. The race server (a small relay) passes moves between phones in real time, but it can’t invent them.
  • Money can’t get stuck. If the relay disappears, every entry can go back to its owner after a timeout the chain enforces, with nobody else’s signature.
  • Sponsored races can’t be farmed. Joining one needs a username cell in your wallet, which the chain checks through a cell dep, and the chain refuses one wallet taking two seats in a prize race.
  • One set of rules everywhere. The race rules are one Rust crate with integer maths only, compiled to RISC-V for CKB-VM and to WebAssembly for the browser and the relay, so all three always agree on who won.
  • Anyone can check it. The results page reads the moves from the finish transaction, replays the race in your browser and checks it against who the chain paid.

Status on testnet

  • live-match (type ID): 0xcf2c00c07441a48baeb76284e8edb8d10c6e016865c3eb6b1f87ad3b57a146b7
  • Latest upgrade, sponsored races (22 Nov): 0x4e13e90f…57d4
  • First sponsored race: a 100 CKB prize, and the winner got their deposit back plus the prize. 70,475,122 cycles: 0x8e3bca44…f623
  • A close entry race on 23 Nov: won by 1.5 seconds with 251 signed moves, and the whole race was replayed on chain before paying 200 CKB. 65,322,821 cycles: 0xcef2e225…d515
  • 49 transaction tests in ckb-testtool on the real RISC-V binaries, plus an OffCKB devnet test of seven full races with a real relay and bot drivers.

The cycle counts above are the chain’s own. You can check them yourself: paste either hash into ckb-cycle-tools. It replays the finish in your browser and splits it per script: for the 23 Nov race, live-match and the game it spawns are 63.5M of the 65.3M (97.3%), and the replay matches the node’s total exactly. The worst case (5 cars, full 3 minutes, twistiest track) is about 141M in my tests.

Things I learned on CKB

  • Spawn and IPC make a game a library. live-match doesn’t know anything about racing. It only asks a game script “who won?”. Any game that serves the same trait could use the same match script and its money rules.
  • Same result everywhere needs integer maths. One float anywhere and the phone and the chain would disagree. Fixed ticks and integer maths keep the browser, the relay and CKB-VM in step.
  • Profile the spawned script on its own. In a spawn, the match script is the parent (VM 0) and the game is a child (VM 1), so a plain profile only sees the parent. With ckb-debugger --vm-id 1 and ckb-cycle-tools, which can profile a spawned script on its own, I found that about half of the game’s cycles go to one function that finds the nearest point on the track. That’s where my next cut goes.
  • A cell dep is a free check. The sponsored-race username pass is read as a cell dep, so it costs the player nothing and the cell isn’t spent.
  • Signing live moves needs ordering. I found that key presses sent as separate web requests could reach the relay out of order. The phone then refused to sign a list it didn’t recognise, and a winner could lose the prize. Now each phone has one WebSocket, and every press is numbered.

What it doesn’t do yet

  • One relay. Only my relay runs races today. It can’t cheat, but if it’s down, races wait for the timeout refund.
  • Reload mid-race: a driver who reloads gets back into the race, but can’t sign the moves made before the reload yet.
  • Usernames are checked as free by the app before you claim one. Making that fully on chain is next.
  • Looks: each car is just its seat’s colour. Car skins you own as Spores, richer environments and real car models are next.

What I’d love feedback on

  • How does racing feel on your phone? Is the steering responsive, and is the lag OK?
  • Is anything confusing for someone new to CKB?
  • About half the replay is a nearest-point search on the track. Has anyone made a search like this cheaper in CKB-VM?
  • Each phone signs its moves with a session key, and the chain checks only the winner’s signature before paying. Do you see a gap in that, or a more CKB-native way to do it?

It’s on testnet. Look for the gold Free entry races: you can join those without paying anything. Or grab some testnet CKB from the faucet and host your own, and share the link with friends: it shows a preview card of the race.

Thanks for reading!
